word.running_title: Human evolution | Evidence and shared origins

blocks.text: **Human evolution is a branching history, not a ladder of progress.** All living people belong to Homo sapiens. We share ancestors with other apes; we did not descend from chimpanzees alive today. [1, 4]

Human evolution describes inherited changes in populations across generations. Mutation introduces variation; selection, chance and movement between populations help shape what persists. Evolution has no intended endpoint. A trait that helps in one environment may be costly in another. [1]

Our history is rooted in Africa. Over millions of years, different hominin populations developed combinations of traits, spread into new environments and sometimes coexisted. Many branches became extinct; their order in a textbook is not proof that one directly became the next. [1, 3]

items: **Walking came early:** bipedalism preceded the large brains of recent humans. [1, 2]
**Traits formed a mosaic:** locomotion, teeth, brains and behaviour did not change all at once. [1–4]
**Some branches reconnected:** ancient DNA demonstrates interbreeding among recent human relatives. [6]

blocks.text: **How to read the dates.** Dates in this brief are approximate and measured before the present. Fossil ranges describe the evidence currently known, not exact biological birthdays or extinction dates. The selected species are examples, not a complete family tree. [1–5]

blocks.alt: Two-panel time-range diagram. The four-million-year panel shows afarensis before erectus, while a 500,000-year zoom shows erectus, Neanderthals and sapiens with overlapping known time ranges. Separate lanes show coexistence, not direct ancestry.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. Original interval infographic from Smithsonian species summaries [2–5]. Each panel has its own labelled linear scale. Separate lanes do not imply ancestry; selected ranges are approximate.

blocks.text: The recent-time zoom matters: long-lived Homo erectus, Neanderthals and early Homo sapiens overlap in the fossil record. Temporal overlap alone does not show that every population met, nor that one species was the direct ancestor of another. Geography and independent evidence are needed. [3–6]

No single fossil tells the whole story. Researchers combine independent evidence, checking whether anatomy, archaeological context, dates and genetics support the same interpretation. Better evidence can revise the interpretation without erasing the broader fact of common ancestry. [1, 6]

blocks.text: **Walking before large brains.** Australopithecus afarensis walked upright but retained long arms and curved fingers associated with climbing. Its small brain and mixed anatomy show why evolution is better understood as a mosaic than a sequence of uniformly improving bodies. [2]

**A wider-ranging way of life.** Homo erectus had relatively long legs and shorter arms, suited to a more ground-based life. Its populations spread beyond Africa. Acheulean handaxes appear during its long history, but the association does not establish that every population used the same technology. [3]
**Interpret carefully:** a trait, tool or fossil age is evidence—not a complete biography, an intelligence score or a guaranteed ancestor–descendant relationship.

Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago. The traits associated with our species include a reorganised skull, lighter skeletal build and increasingly varied behaviours. These features should not be treated as a single switch that flipped at one instant. Our direct ancestry and the relationships among some fossil populations remain debated. [1, 4]

Homo sapiens eventually spread widely, encountering other human relatives. Earlier Homo dispersal and later sapiens dispersal are different chapters; neither is adequately represented by one universal arrow on a map. This brief avoids exact migration dates where routes, timing and surviving ancestry require more detailed treatment. [1, 3, 6]

**Neanderthals were not failed modern humans.** They were a distinct, closely related Eurasian branch, with sophisticated tools, fire use and adaptations to demanding environments. Their disappearance by roughly 40,000 years ago does not mean they were simply unintelligent or culturally empty. [5]

**DNA changes the picture.** Ancient genomes demonstrate interbreeding involving Homo sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans. Branches that diverged could later exchange genes. Ancestry varies across individuals and populations; it is not a ranking of human worth or a measure of how evolved someone is. [6]

**Culture is not a biological finish line.** Art, technology and social learning have deep histories. Food production developed only within the past roughly 12,000 years, long after our species appeared. Biological evolution and cultural change operate on different mechanisms and timescales. [1, 4]

**What remains open:** exact ancestor–descendant links, the full diversity of ancient populations, and the timing and spread of some behaviours. Language leaves no direct fossil record; it should not be assigned a confident birthday from one bone or gene. [1, 4, 6]

**Takeaway:** shared ancestry, diverse adaptations and occasional reconnection explain the evidence better than a straight march toward perfection. Every living human population has an equally long evolutionary history.

Numbered references below match the claim markers throughout the brief and slide notes. All six source pages were read on 1 October 2026. These are authoritative museum summaries rather than an exhaustive literature review; contested details are kept qualified.

**Visual provenance.** The infographic is an original illustration generated from the cited approximate ranges. It contains no borrowed photographs, fossil reconstructions or licensed template art. PNG is provided for immediate use; SVG preserves scalable text and geometry for editing.

**Scope.** General-audience overview, selective species coverage, no claim of a complete phylogeny. Dates may change as evidence improves. This document separates the stated species ranges from inferred divergence dates and does not equate brain size with intelligence.

slides.notes: Explain common ancestry without implying that chimpanzees alive today were our ancestors. Hominins refers here to humans and extinct relatives on our branch. Evolution has no goal or ranking of living populations. [1,4]

slides.notes: Myr = million years; kyr = thousand years. These are rounded anchors, not exact boundaries. Approximately six million years is a broad teaching frame, not a precise estimate of every lineage split. The species range and food-production date follow Smithsonian summaries. [1,4]

slides.title: Several human relatives overlapped in time
slides.alt: Separate horizontal lanes show approximate ranges for afarensis, erectus, Neanderthals and sapiens. A recent-time zoom makes coexistence visible. No lane implies direct ancestry.
slides.caption: Selected fossil ranges; two labelled scales. Overlap does not prove contact or direct ancestry.
slides.notes: The left axis covers four million years; the right zoom covers the last 500,000 years. Both are linear within their own panel. Known ranges are approximate. Afarensis is not presented as a proven direct ancestor, and overlap alone does not demonstrate contact. [2,3,4,5]

slides.title: Independent evidence makes the story testable

right.heading: Genetics + its limits
bullets: Warm conditions often destroy ancient DNA.

slides.source: Smithsonian evidence overview and ancient DNA [1, 6]
slides.notes: No one evidence stream is complete. Anatomy can reveal locomotion; archaeological objects require context and do not always identify their maker. DNA preservation creates a strong sampling bias. Comparing independent observations is more reliable than treating one fossil as a complete story. [1,6]

slides.title: Upright walking came before very large brains

right.heading: Why this matters
bullets: Human traits did not arrive together.
A sequence of fossils is not a ladder.

slides.notes: Afarensis had long arms and curved fingers along with regular bipedal walking. Avoid depicting it as half a modern human or a guaranteed direct ancestor. Its mixed anatomy is the point, not a judgment of intelligence. [2]

slides.title: Homo erectus expanded the range of human life
bullets: **Longer legs and shorter arms** suited a ground-based life.
Populations spread beyond Africa into parts of Asia.
Handaxes appear during its long history.
Regional diversity complicates a single species story.
slides.notes: The source's stated known range is about 1.89 million to 110,000 years ago; older narrative text on the same page gives a different late date, so use the summary range consistently. Some researchers distinguish African ergaster from Asian erectus. Tool and fire associations do not justify a single confident invention date for every population. [3]

slides.title: Homo sapiens emerged in Africa—not fully formed
bullets: Our species appears about **300,000 years ago**.
Anatomy and behaviour changed over time.
Later dispersal connected widely separated populations.
slides.notes: Do not turn the approximate species range into a claim of one founding individual or one sudden behavioural revolution. Earlier Homo migrations and later sapiens dispersal are separate histories. This brief does not assign a single universal departure date from Africa. [1,4]

slides.title: Different branches sometimes exchanged genes

left.heading: Neanderthals
bullets: A distinct, closely related Eurasian branch.

right.heading: What ancient DNA shows
bullets: Ancestry is not a measure of human worth.

slides.notes: Neanderthals were not failed versions of us. DNA establishes gene flow among sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans. Avoid a single ancestry percentage for everyone, and do not assume all people in overlapping time ranges actually met. [5,6]

slides.title: The strongest account names what remains uncertain

left.heading: Well supported
bullets: Common ancestry and deep African roots.
Gene flow among some recent branches.

right.heading: Still under study
bullets: Exact links among some fossil populations.
Timing and spread of certain behaviours.

slides.notes: Distinguish uncertainty about specific relationships from uncertainty about evolution itself. Language cannot be assigned a confident birthday from one gene or bone. Dates and taxonomic labels can change as new evidence appears. [1,4,6]

slides.text:
The evidence tells a story of adaptation,
diversity and connection—not perfection.
slides.notes: End with three takeaways: evolution branches; traits form a mosaic; all living people are one species with shared ancestry. Invite questions about the evidence and what remains unresolved. [1–6]
